quiz.explain: The last western emperor was deposed in 476.

lessons.title: The Middle Ages
lessons.summary: Castles, monasteries, knights and plague.

cards.title: A thousand years
cards.text: The Middle Ages run roughly from the fall of Rome (476) to the late 1400s. The name was coined later by Renaissance thinkers who saw it as a gap between antiquity and their own time.

deep.x: Italian writers like Petrarch, in the 1300s, saw a glorious ancient past, then a long gloomy time, then a revival in their own day. The term "Middle Ages" (medium aevum) took hold in the 1400s–1600s for that middle period.
Three stages

Historians usually split the period. The early centuries saw fewer and smaller towns in the west. After about 1000, population, trade, towns and building boomed, until famine and plague struck in the 1300s.
When did it end?
There's no single date. Historians choose different markers depending on what they study.
The whole story of how Portugal was born, from county to kingdom to Aljubarrota, happened in the Middle Ages.
"Middle Ages" is a label invented by people who looked down on it; the period itself was a thousand years of change.

cards.title: Feudalism
cards.text: Land was the main source of wealth. Kings granted land to lords in return for military service; peasants worked the land for lords in return for protection.

deep.x: After Rome's fall, there was little money and few strong states. Rulers paid for soldiers with the one thing they had: land. A lord promised loyalty and service; in return his lord granted him a **fief**, land plus the peasants who worked it.
Life on the manor

Serfs weren't slaves, but they were tied to the land. They farmed their own strips and owed the lord work, often several days a week, plus payments in grain, eggs or money. They also paid a tithe to the Church.
Portugal was different

Portuguese kings stayed strong, partly because the Reconquista made them war leaders. Many towns received a **foral**, a royal charter setting out their rights and taxes, which limited what lords could demand.

deep.w: Feudalism was a neat pyramid everywhere
deep.r: It was messy and varied by region; the word "feudalism" was coined centuries later, and historians debate how useful it is

deep.x: In a world without much money, land was how you paid for loyalty.

cards.title: The Church
cards.text: The Catholic Church was the most powerful institution in western Europe: it owned land, ran schools and hospitals, kept learning alive in monasteries and shaped daily life.

deep.x: The Church touched everything: birth (baptism), marriage, death and burial. Bells marked the hours, saints' days set the calendar, and the parish priest was often the only local person who could read.
Monasteries

Monks following the Rule of St Benedict, written around 530, divided the day between prayer, work and study. In scriptoria they copied Latin texts, including pagan classics that might otherwise have been lost. Monasteries also ran farms, schools and guest houses for travellers.

x: Alcobaça, founded in 1153 by Cistercian monks, was given land by Afonso Henriques
Its monks drained marshes and spread new farming techniques

deep.x: Wealth and power

x: A farmer harvests 200 sacks of grain
tithe = one-tenth
20 sacks go to the Church

deep.x: Its wealth also caused scandals and calls for reform, which would eventually lead to the Reformation.
In 1054 the Latin west and Greek east excommunicated each other, splitting Catholic and Orthodox churches; the split still exists.
The medieval Church was church, school, hospital, landlord and record office all at once.

cards.title: Castles
cards.text: Castles were fortified homes and military bases. Portugal has hundreds, many built or rebuilt during the Reconquista: Guimarães, Almourol, Óbidos, Marvão.

deep.x: Castles spread across Europe from the 900s, as local lords needed strongholds. Early ones were earth mounds with wooden towers. From the 1100s, stone castles with tall keeps and thick walls became common.
Built to make attackers suffer

x: Battlements let defenders shoot and then duck
Arrow slits were narrow outside, wide inside
Gates had drawbridges, portcullises and holes above to drop things through

deep.x: Portugal's castles
Many frontier castles were built by the Templars under Gualdim Pais, who also founded Tomar in 1160. King Dinis rebuilt dozens along the border with Castile.
The end of castles

Gunpowder cannons, common from the 1400s, smashed high walls. Engineers replaced castles with low, thick, star-shaped forts. The fortifications of Elvas, a UNESCO site, are among the largest of this kind in the world.
Since King Dinis gave it to his wife Isabel in 1282, the town of Óbidos was traditionally a wedding gift to Portuguese queens.
Castles were built for a world of swords and arrows, and cannons made them romantic ruins.

cards.title: Crusades
cards.text: From 1096, Christian armies launched crusades to take Jerusalem and the Holy Land. Crusaders also helped Afonso Henriques conquer Lisbon in 1147 on their way east.

deep.x: In 1095, Pope Urban II called on western knights to help the Byzantine Empire against the Seljuk Turks and to take Jerusalem. Fighters were promised forgiveness of sins.
The siege of Lisbon

In 1147 a fleet of crusaders from England, Flanders and the Rhineland stopped in Porto on their way to the Holy Land. The bishop of Porto persuaded them to help Afonso Henriques besiege Lisbon, in return for loot.
An Englishman, Gilbert of Hastings, became Lisbon's first bishop after the conquest.
Consequences
In Iberia, popes granted crusade status to the Reconquista, and military orders like the Templars and the Order of Avis received land for defending the frontier.

deep.w: The crusades were only about faith
deep.r: Faith mattered, but so did land, plunder, trade, family honour and politics, as Lisbon showed

deep.x: Lisbon became Portuguese partly because crusaders heading east took a profitable detour.

cards.title: The Black Death
cards.text: Plague swept Europe from 1347, carried by fleas on rats and spread between people. It killed perhaps a third to a half of Europe's population within a few years.

deep.x: The plague is caused by the bacterium Yersinia pestis, which lives in wild rodents. It arrived in Europe in 1347 on ships from the Black Sea and spread along trade routes, reaching Portugal in 1348.
Three forms

x: Bubonic: swollen, painful lymph nodes (buboes); many died within a week
Pneumonic: in the lungs, spread by coughing, almost always fatal
Septicaemic: in the blood, killing fastest of all

deep.x: Some researchers now think human fleas and lice also spread it between people, helping explain how fast it moved.
Responses

Nobody knew about bacteria. People blamed bad air, the stars or God's anger. Some groups whipped themselves in public; others attacked Jewish communities, falsely accused of poisoning wells. Ragusa (Dubrovnik) and then Venice developed isolation for arriving ships.

x: Ships made to wait 30 days, later 40
Italian "quaranta giorni" = 40 days
→ the word "quarantine"

deep.x: The plague kept returning for centuries; one of the last big western European outbreaks hit Marseille in 1720.
The Black Death was the deadliest pandemic in European history, and quarantine was one of its lasting lessons.

cards.title: After the plague
cards.text: With so many workers dead, survivors could demand higher wages and more freedom. Serfdom weakened in western Europe, and new ideas took root.

deep.x: The plague killed people but left land, tools and buildings intact. Suddenly there were too few workers for the work, and labour became valuable.
Lords fight back
Governments tried to force wages back to pre-plague levels. In Portugal, King Fernando's **Lei das Sesmarias** of 1375 ordered idle land to be farmed and pushed labourers back to the fields.
A divided Europe

Ordinary survivors in the west often ate more meat, drank more ale and wore better clothes than their grandparents. Some economists argue high wages encouraged labour-saving inventions in later centuries.
A darker mood
Art turned to death: skeletons dancing with kings and peasants, the "dance of death", reminded everyone that death came for all.

deep.w: Things went back to normal after the plague
deep.r: Society changed for good: in western Europe, peasants gained freedoms that lords could never fully take back

deep.x: When labour became scarce, ordinary people gained bargaining power for the first time in centuries.

cards.title: Gothic cathedrals
cards.text: From the 1100s, pointed arches, ribbed vaults and flying buttresses let builders raise tall, light cathedrals with huge stained-glass windows. The Batalha monastery is a Portuguese masterpiece.

deep.x: Gothic began at the abbey of Saint-Denis near Paris in the 1140s. Builders wanted churches full of light, which they saw as a symbol of God. The problem: big windows weaken walls. Gothic engineering solved it.
Height records
Builders pushed too far sometimes: part of Beauvais' vault collapsed in 1284.
Batalha

Begun in 1386, the Monastery of Batalha was designed first by Afonso Domingues, then by a master called Huguet. Its Founder's Chapel holds the tombs of João I and Philippa of Lancaster. Its "Unfinished Chapels" were never roofed.

x: Stained-glass windows taught Bible stories to people who couldn't read
Many cathedrals took over a century to build; Cologne's was finished only in 1880

deep.x: Notre-Dame in Paris burned in 2019 and reopened in December 2024 after a huge restoration.
Gothic builders turned stone into light by pushing its weight outside the walls.

cards.title: Universities
cards.text: Europe's first universities appeared in Bologna (1088), Paris and Oxford. Portugal's university was founded in Lisbon in 1290 and later moved permanently to Coimbra in 1537.

deep.x: A medieval university wasn't a campus; it was a **universitas**, a guild of students or teachers who organised to protect their interests, like any trade guild. At Bologna, students hired and fined their professors.
What students learned
Teaching was in Latin. Students started with the seven liberal arts, then could move to higher faculties.
Teaching was by lecture, where a master read and explained a text, and by disputation, a formal debate on a question. Degrees were bachelor, master and doctor, titles still used today.
Portugal's university
King Dinis founded a "Estudo Geral" in Lisbon in 1290. It moved between Lisbon and Coimbra several times before King João III settled it in Coimbra for good in 1537.
In Coimbra's 18th-century Joanina Library, a colony of small bats eats insects that would damage the old books; staff cover the tables at night.
The university began as a medieval guild, and its degrees, gowns and debates are still with us.

cards.title: The medieval world wasn't "dark"
cards.text: The Middle Ages brought windmills, eyeglasses, mechanical clocks, the compass in Europe, universities and great art. The idea of "dark ages" is now seen as too simple.

deep.x: The label "Dark Ages" came from Renaissance writers who admired ancient Rome, and from later critics of the Church. Today historians see the period as one of real invention and growth.
Farming advances

x: The heavy plough turned heavy northern soils
The horse collar let horses pull without choking
Three-field rotation left only a third of land fallow, not half

deep.x: These raised food production and helped Europe's population roughly double between 1000 and 1300.
Culture
Medieval Europe produced Dante, Chaucer, Gothic cathedrals and the universities. In Iberia, poet-kings wrote songs: King Dinis was one of the finest troubadour poets in Galician-Portuguese.
The 1086 Domesday survey of England counted about 5,600 watermills, roughly one for every few hundred people.
The Middle Ages were dark only to those who weren't looking.

quiz.q: What killed perhaps a third of Europe in the 1300s?
Who helped Afonso Henriques take Lisbon in 1147?
Where did Portugal's university settle permanently in 1537?
quiz.explain: It moved between Lisbon and Coimbra before settling.

lessons.title: Al-Andalus
lessons.summary: Muslim Iberia and the Islamic golden age.

cards.title: 711: a new era in Iberia

events.l: most of Iberia under Muslim rule

cards.text: In 711, Muslim armies from North Africa crossed into Iberia and within a few years controlled most of the peninsula, including today's Portugal. They called it al-Andalus.

deep.x: In 711 a commander called **Tariq ibn Ziyad** crossed the strait from North Africa with an army of perhaps 7,000–12,000 men, most of them Berbers rather than Arabs. The rock where he landed still carries his name: Jabal Tariq, "Tariq's mountain", which became Gibraltar.
Why it was so fast

The Visigothic kingdom was divided. Its king, Roderic, had just taken the throne in a disputed succession, and his rivals may even have helped the invaders. Roderic died at the Battle of Guadalete, and many towns surrendered by treaty, keeping their property and religion in exchange for tribute.
Who ruled

At first al-Andalus was a far-western province of the Umayyad caliphate, ruled from Damascus. When the Umayyads were overthrown in 750, a surviving prince, Abd al-Rahman I, escaped to Iberia and set up an independent emirate in Córdoba in 756.

x: The far north, around Asturias, was never conquered
Tradition dates the first Christian victory to Covadonga, around 722
The name al-Andalus may echo the Vandals, but its origin is still debated

deep.w: The Arabs swept in and replaced the population
deep.r: Most people stayed; over generations many converted and learnt Arabic, while a small Arab and Berber elite ruled

deep.x: The conquest of 711 was quick because a divided kingdom gave way, not because Iberia was emptied and refilled.

cards.title: Córdoba
cards.text: In the 10th century Córdoba was one of Europe's largest and most sophisticated cities, with paved streets, lighting, baths, libraries and the great mosque.

deep.x: Under Abd al-Rahman III, who declared himself caliph in 929, Córdoba became the capital of the richest state in western Europe. Population estimates vary widely, from about 100,000 to several hundred thousand, but it was certainly far bigger than Paris or London at the time.
The Great Mosque

Building began in 785 and was enlarged by later rulers until it held a forest of more than 800 columns, topped by striped red-and-white double arches. Some columns were reused from Roman and Visigothic buildings.
City life

x: Running water from restored Roman aqueducts and many public baths
Markets selling silk, leather, paper and ivory
The library of caliph al-Hakam II, said to hold hundreds of thousands of books (the number is probably exaggerated)
A palace-city, Madinat al-Zahra, built just outside town

deep.x: The philosophers Averroes (Ibn Rushd) and Maimonides, a Muslim and a Jew, were both born in Córdoba in the 1120s–1130s.
For about a century, Córdoba was the place western Europe looked to for luxury, learning and power.

cards.title: Three faiths
cards.text: Muslims, Christians and Jews lived side by side in al-Andalus, with Christians and Jews as protected but taxed minorities. Coexistence was real but not equality, and it varied over time.

deep.x: Islamic law treated Christians and Jews as **dhimmis**, "protected people" of the Book. They could keep their religion, property and own courts, but paid a special tax (the jizya) and faced limits: no new churches, no public processions, no authority over Muslims.

items.b: ruling faith, a minority at first

deep.x: A changing picture

Over centuries, conversion slowly turned Muslims into the majority. Some Christians and Jews rose high: the Jewish doctor Hasdai ibn Shaprut served as a diplomat for Abd al-Rahman III. But tensions flared too. In the 850s about 48 Christians in Córdoba were executed after deliberately insulting Islam, and in 1066 a mob in Granada killed many Jews.
Harder times

From the late 1000s, rulers from North Africa, the Almoravids and then the Almohads, were far stricter. Maimonides' family fled Córdoba in the 1140s. The Christian kingdoms, for their part, later forced Jews and Muslims to convert or leave.

deep.w: Al-Andalus was a paradise of tolerance
deep.r: It allowed more diversity than most of Europe then, but within a clear hierarchy, and conditions changed a lot over time

deep.x: Al-Andalus offered protection, not equality, and that was unusual enough for its time.

cards.title: Islamic golden age
cards.text: From roughly the 8th to 13th centuries, scholars in Baghdad, Cairo and Córdoba translated and extended Greek, Persian and Indian knowledge in mathematics, astronomy, medicine and philosophy.

deep.x: From the 700s the Abbasid caliphs in Baghdad paid for the translation of Greek, Persian and Indian works into Arabic. A centre often called the **House of Wisdom** gathered scholars. They didn't just copy; they tested, corrected and added.
Big names

Ibn Sina's Canon of Medicine was still a textbook in European universities in the 1600s. Ibn al-Haytham showed that we see because light enters the eye, not because the eye sends out rays, and insisted on testing ideas with experiments.
Paper made it possible

Papermaking reached the Islamic world from China in the 700s; Baghdad had paper mills by about 800. Cheap paper made books far more common than in Christian Europe. One of Europe's first paper mills worked at Xàtiva, near Valencia, under Muslim rule.
The route to Europe
After Castile took Toledo in 1085, translators there turned Arabic books into Latin. Gerard of Cremona alone translated dozens of works, including Ptolemy's astronomy and Ibn Sina.
Many star names, like Aldebaran, Betelgeuse and Rigel, come from Arabic.
Much of the "rediscovery" of Greek science in medieval Europe arrived by way of Arabic.

cards.title: Numbers we use
cards.text: The digits 0–9 came from India, reached Europe through the Arab world and are called Hindu-Arabic numerals. The word "algorithm" comes from al-Khwarizmi's name.

deep.x: Indian mathematicians developed a system with just nine digits plus a sign for zero, where a digit's **place** sets its value. By 628 the astronomer Brahmagupta was writing rules for calculating with zero as a number.
Why place value wins
Roman numerals have no zero and no place value, so written sums are awkward. With Hindu-Arabic digits you can add, multiply and keep accounts on paper, which merchants and bankers loved.

x: 1,888 in Roman numerals
MDCCCLXXXVIII
13 symbols instead of 4

deep.x: The man behind the words

Al-Khwarizmi wrote a book explaining Indian reckoning around 825. Its Latin translation began "Algoritmi dicit…", "Al-Khwarizmi says…", and his name became **algorithm**. His other book, on "al-jabr" (restoring), gave us **algebra**.
Change was slow. Some European cities, worried about fraud, banned the new digits in official accounts in the 1200s, because a 0 could easily be changed into a 6 or 9.
In Portuguese a digit is an **algarismo**, a word that comes straight from al-Khwarizmi's name.
The numbers on every price tag travelled from India through Baghdad and al-Andalus before reaching Portugal.

cards.title: Agriculture and irrigation
cards.text: Muslim farmers introduced or spread crops like oranges, lemons, rice, almonds and sugar cane in Iberia, along with irrigation systems such as the water wheel (nora).

deep.x: Al-Andalus drew on farming know-how from across the Islamic world, from Persia to Egypt. Andalusi agronomists like Ibn al-Awwam wrote detailed manuals on grafting, soils and watering.
Lifting water

The **nora** is a wheel with clay pots (alcatruzes) tied to it. Turned by a donkey or a mule, it lifts water from a well and tips it into channels (acéquias). Small dams (açudes) held river water back. Portuguese farmers used noras well into the 20th century.
Summer crops
Many new crops needed water in the hot, dry summer. Irrigation let farmers grow a second harvest, so the same field fed more people. That supported bigger towns like Córdoba and Seville.

deep.w: The Arabs brought the sweet orange
deep.r: They brought the bitter orange; the sweet orange arrived around 1500, partly via Portuguese traders, which is why Greeks call it "portokali"

deep.x: Valencia's Water Tribunal, which settles irrigation disputes every Thursday by the cathedral door, is said to go back to Andalusi times.
Irrigation turned dry southern Iberia into a garden that could grow crops all year.

cards.title: Arabic in Portuguese
cards.text: Portuguese has hundreds of words of Arabic origin, often starting with "al-": azeite, arroz, alface, almofada, açúcar, aldeia, armazém. "Oxalá" comes from "if God wills".

deep.x: After Latin, Arabic gave Portuguese more words than any other language in the Middle Ages, with estimates from several hundred to around a thousand. Most are **nouns** for things that were new or traded: food, farming, building, trade and government.
Why so many start with "a"
"Al" means "the" in Arabic. Portuguese speakers heard it as part of the word. Before certain consonants Arabic changes al- to as-, az- or ar-, which is why we get açúcar and arroz.
What didn't change
Grammar, verbs and everyday basics like "pai", "água" and "comer" stayed Latin. Arabic added vocabulary, not structure. Even "fulano", meaning "so-and-so", comes from Arabic fulan.

deep.w: Every word starting with "al-" is Arabic
deep.r: Many aren't: almoço comes from Latin, and alto from Latin altus

deep.x: Spanish and Portuguese often share the same Arabic words, while Italian or French use Latin ones: "azeite" but "olio", "huile".
Portuguese is Latin in its bones, with Arabic woven into its kitchen, house and market.

cards.title: Place names
cards.text: Many Portuguese places have Arabic names: the Algarve (al-gharb, "the west"), Alcácer, Alfama, Albufeira, Fátima (a Muslim name).

deep.x: Place names are like fossils: they keep old languages long after people stop speaking them. Southern Portugal is especially rich in Arabic names.
Rivers and towns

The Arabic **wadi**, "river" or "valley", turns up as "Ode-" or "Guadi-": Odemira, Odeceixe, Odivelas and the Guadiana, which mixes wadi with the Roman river name Anas. Coimbra's Arco de Almedina comes from al-madina, "the town".
Fátima

Fatima was the name of the Prophet Muhammad's daughter, popular among Muslims. A local legend says a Moorish girl named Fátima was captured by a Christian knight, married him and converted, taking the name Oureana, which gave nearby Ourém its name. It's a legend, but the place name is real evidence of the Muslim past.

deep.w: The north has no Arabic place names
deep.r: They are rarer, since Muslim rule there was shorter, but some exist, like Alfândega da Fé

deep.x: Lisbon's Mouraria neighbourhood is where Muslims were made to live after the city's conquest in 1147.
Read a map of the Algarve and you're reading Arabic.

cards.title: The Reconquista
cards.text: Christian kingdoms in the north gradually pushed south over nearly 800 years. Portugal completed its reconquest with the Algarve in 1249; Spain with Granada in 1492.

deep.x: The word **Reconquista** ("reconquest") was coined much later and is debated by historians, because it suggests a single planned campaign. In reality it was nearly 800 years of advances, truces, alliances and civil wars on both sides.
How the frontier moved

When al-Andalus split into small rival kingdoms (taifas) after 1031, Christian kings forced them to pay tribute called parias. North African dynasties then came in twice to reunite the south and push back. The great Christian victory at Las Navas de Tolosa in 1212 broke Almohad power.
Allies across faiths
El Cid, Castile's hero, also fought for the Muslim king of Zaragoza. Alfonso VI of Castile took a Muslim princess, Zaida of Seville, as a partner, and Muslim rulers often hired Christian soldiers.

x: almost eight centuries

deep.x: Portugal finished its reconquest 243 years before Spain, which is one reason it was free to look to the sea earlier.
The Reconquista was a long, messy shifting of borders, not a single crusade.

cards.title: Silves and Mértola
cards.text: Silves was the capital of the Algarve under Muslim rule, and Mértola's church was once a mosque. Both still show their Islamic past in walls, streets and museums.

deep.x: Silves

Called **Xelb** (Shilb), Silves was the main city of the Algarve under Muslim rule, famous for its poets and gardens. Its red sandstone castle still looms over the town, and an Almohad cistern inside it once stored water for a siege. Sancho I took the city in 1189 with crusaders' help, lost it two years later, and Portugal took it for good in the 1240s.
Mértola

Mértola sits on a steep hill above the Guadiana, which was a river port for Roman and Islamic traders. In 1144 a Sufi leader, Ibn Qasi, launched a revolt from here. The main church was the town mosque. It still has the **mihrab**, the niche facing Mecca, and the forest of columns inside echoes a mosque's prayer hall.

x: Mértola calls itself a "Vila Museu", with small museums of Islamic art and ceramics
It holds an Islamic Festival every two years
Silves has an archaeology museum built around a deep Islamic well

deep.x: Al-Mu'tamid, a poet-king of Seville born in Beja, governed Silves as a young man and later wrote longingly about its palace.
In Silves and Mértola, al-Andalus isn't in a textbook; you can walk through it.

quiz.q: What did Muslims call Iberia?
The word "algorithm" comes from…
When did Portugal complete its reconquest?

lessons.title: The birth of Portugal
lessons.summary: From county to kingdom, and the battle that saved it.

cards.title: The County of Portucale
cards.text: Portugal began as a county of the kingdom of León, named after Portucale, today's Porto area. In 1096 it was given to Henry of Burgundy and his wife Teresa.

deep.x: The name **Portucale** joined two places on the Douro: Portus (a port on the north bank, today's Porto) and Cale (on the south bank, near Gaia). In 868 a nobleman, Vímara Peres, took the area back from Muslim control and it became a county, a territory run by a count for the king of León.
Henry and Teresa

Around 1096 King Alfonso VI of León and Castile gave the county to **Henry of Burgundy**, a French knight who had come to fight the Muslims. Henry married Teresa, Alfonso's daughter (born outside marriage). The county stretched roughly from the Minho to around Coimbra.
Teresa rules alone

Henry died in 1112. Teresa ruled the county and called herself "queen". She grew close to a powerful Galician noble, Fernão Peres de Trava, which worried Portuguese barons who feared being swallowed by Galicia.

deep.w: Portugal was founded by a Portuguese hero against foreigners
deep.r: Its founders were a French count and a Leonese princess, and the early fight was a family and noble power struggle

deep.x: Portugal began as a frontier county on the Douro, granted by one king to a foreign knight.

cards.title: São Mamede, 1128
cards.text: Young Afonso Henriques defeated his mother Teresa's forces at the Battle of São Mamede near Guimarães in 1128, taking control of the county. Guimarães is called "the cradle of Portugal".

deep.x: On 24 June 1128, near Guimarães, the young **Afonso Henriques**, then about 17–20 years old, beat the forces of his mother Teresa and her ally Fernão Peres de Trava. Teresa left for Galicia, where she died two years later.
Why it mattered
It was a modest battle, but it put power in the hands of a ruler backed by the local nobility. From then on Afonso pushed for independence from León and expansion south against the Muslims.
The cradle

Guimarães was the county's main seat. Its castle and the Palace of the Dukes of Braganza sit on the "sacred hill", and a section of the old town wall bears the words "Aqui nasceu Portugal", "Portugal was born here".

x: Afonso's exact birth year and place are uncertain; Guimarães, Viseu and Coimbra all claim him
Tradition says he was baptised in the small church of São Miguel by the castle

deep.x: A later legend says Afonso even chained up his mother; it's a chroniclers' story with little evidence.
At São Mamede a son beat his mother, and a county started on the road to being a kingdom.

cards.title: Recognition: 1143 and 1179
cards.text: At the Treaty of Zamora (1143), Alfonso VII of León recognised Afonso as king. The Pope formally confirmed it in 1179 with the bull Manifestis Probatum.

deep.x: Medieval kingdoms needed recognition. After victories such as **Ourique** (1139), Afonso began calling himself king. In 1143, at Zamora, his cousin Alfonso VII of León, who called himself "emperor of Spain", accepted Afonso's royal title, with a papal envoy present.
Going over León's head

Afonso then declared himself a vassal of the Pope and promised an annual tribute of gold. This was clever: owing loyalty directly to Rome meant not owing it to León. The Popes delayed for decades, but in 1179 Alexander III issued the bull **Manifestis Probatum**, calling Afonso king and his land a kingdom.
Why the Pope agreed
Afonso had proved useful: he had taken Lisbon and pushed far south against Muslim rulers, which the Church saw as a crusade. Money and military success made the case.
The Treaty of Zamora is traditionally dated 5 October 1143, the same day of the year the Portuguese Republic was proclaimed in 1910.
Portugal became a kingdom in two steps: a neighbour's nod in 1143 and the Pope's seal in 1179.

cards.title: Moving south
cards.text: Afonso and his successors took Santarém and Lisbon (1147), then the Alentejo and finally the Algarve (1249). Portugal's borders, set by the Treaty of Alcañices in 1297, are among Europe's oldest.

deep.x: Expansion was both conquest and settlement. Kings granted land and charters (forais) to attract settlers, and military orders such as the Templars, Hospitallers and Order of Santiago held frontier castles.
Lisbon, 1147

Santarém fell to a surprise night attack in March 1147. That summer, a fleet of crusaders from England, Flanders and Germany, sailing to the Holy Land, stopped in Porto and agreed to help. After a siege of about 17 weeks, Lisbon surrendered in October. The crusaders were paid in plunder, and some stayed.
Setbacks
In 1169 Afonso was wounded and captured at Badajoz, and the Almohads fought back hard in the 1190s. It took four more kings to reach the coast of the Algarve: Afonso III took Faro in 1249.
Fixed borders

In 1297 King Dinis and Castile signed the Treaty of Alcañices. Portugal gained the Riba-Côa area, and the land border has barely moved since, apart from the disputed town of Olivença, taken by Spain in 1801.
Portugal's land border with Spain is about 1,200 km long and one of the oldest stable borders in Europe.
In about 150 years Portugal reached the south coast, and then kept the same shape for more than seven centuries.

cards.title: King Dinis
cards.text: Dom Dinis (reigned 1279–1325) planted the pine forest of Leiria to protect farmland and supply timber, founded the university, made Portuguese the official language of documents and created the Order of Christ.

deep.x: Dom Dinis came to the throne in 1279 at 17. With the reconquest finished, he could focus on building the country. He was nicknamed **o Lavrador**, "the Farmer", and also "the Poet King".
Order of Christ

When the Pope dissolved the Templars in 1312, many kings seized their wealth. Dinis instead created a new order, the **Order of Christ**, in 1319, and handed it the Templars' castles and lands. A century later its money would help pay for Henry the Navigator's voyages, and its red cross flew on the sails.
Land and sea

He set up fairs, protected farmers, rebuilt dozens of castles along the border and hired a Genoese admiral, Manuel Pessanha, in 1317 to organise a navy. The pine forest near Leiria held back moving sand dunes and later supplied timber for ships.
A poet king
Dinis wrote more than 130 songs (cantigas) in Galician-Portuguese, many of them love songs in a woman's voice. His wife, Isabel of Aragon, became a saint, the Rainha Santa of Coimbra.
About 86% of the Pinhal de Leiria burned in the fires of October 2017; replanting is still under way.
Dinis turned a conquered territory into a working kingdom with its own language, schools and forests.

cards.title: The 1383–85 crisis
cards.text: When King Fernando died without a son, Castile claimed the throne. Many Portuguese backed João, Master of Avis. The crisis became a fight for independence.

deep.x: King Fernando died in October 1383. His only heir was his daughter **Beatriz**, aged about 10 and married to Juan I of Castile. If she inherited, Portugal could become part of Castile. Fernando's widow, Leonor Teles, ruled as regent, influenced by a Galician noble, Count Andeiro.
Who backed whom

In December 1383 João, Master of the military Order of Avis and Fernando's half-brother born outside marriage, killed Andeiro in the palace. Lisbon's people rose in support. Much of the high nobility, however, sided with Castile.
Holding on

Castile besieged Lisbon by land and sea in 1384, but plague broke out in its camp and the army withdrew. Meanwhile the young commander Nuno Álvares Pereira won at Atoleiros in the Alentejo. In April 1385 the Cortes in Coimbra chose João as king, after the lawyer João das Regras argued that the throne was vacant.
Most of what we know comes from Fernão Lopes, a royal chronicler writing about 50 years later, who gave unusual attention to ordinary townspeople.
The crisis turned a succession quarrel into the first moment of Portuguese national identity.

cards.title: Aljubarrota, 1385
cards.text: On 14 August 1385, a smaller Portuguese army under Nuno Álvares Pereira and King João I, with English archers, defeated Castile at Aljubarrota using defensive tactics. Independence was secured.

deep.x: Juan I of Castile invaded with a large army, including heavy French cavalry. João I and Nuno Álvares chose to wait for them on ground they had picked, near Aljubarrota, between Leiria and Alcobaça.
Defensive tactics

The Portuguese stood on foot on a small plateau, with streams protecting the flanks. In front they dug ditches and hidden pits, and English archers shot from the sides. These were the same ideas the English used against the French at Crécy and Poitiers.

The Castilian army arrived tired, late in the afternoon of 14 August, and attacked a narrow front. Charging knights fell into the ditches and were cut down. Juan I fled to Santarém and then by sea to Seville.

deep.w: Brites de Almeida killed seven Castilians with her baker's shovel
deep.r: It's a much-loved later legend, not a documented event

deep.x: Numbers for both armies are estimates from chroniclers; historians agree only that Portugal was heavily outnumbered.
At Aljubarrota good ground and discipline beat sheer numbers, and Portugal stayed independent.

cards.title: Batalha monastery
cards.text: João I built the Monastery of Santa Maria da Vitória at Batalha to give thanks for Aljubarrota. It's a UNESCO World Heritage site and a masterpiece of Gothic and Manueline art.

deep.x: João I had vowed to build a monastery to the Virgin if he won. Work began in 1386 at a site a few kilometres from the battlefield, and the town that grew around it took the name **Batalha**, simply "battle".
Highlights

The Chapter House roof is a star vault about 19 m across with no central support. Legend says the architect, Afonso Domingues, now blind, sat under it for three days to prove it would not fall. It now holds the tomb of Portugal's Unknown Soldiers from the First World War, with a guard of honour.
Unfinished forever

King Duarte began a second burial chapel, but later kings moved their money and attention to the Jerónimos in Lisbon. So the Unfinished Chapels still stand open to the sky, with huge carved Manueline doorways.
Henry the Navigator and his brothers lie in the Founder's Chapel, beside their parents.
Batalha is a battle turned into stone: a thank-you that took more than a century to build.

cards.title: The oldest alliance

events.l: João I marries Philippa of Lancaster

cards.text: The Treaty of Windsor (1386) between Portugal and England is the oldest diplomatic alliance in the world still in force. João I married Philippa of Lancaster, mother of Prince Henry the Navigator.

deep.x: Portugal and England first made an alliance in 1373. After Aljubarrota, where English archers had fought, they signed the **Treaty of Windsor** on 9 May 1386, promising "perpetual friendship" and mutual help.
A royal marriage

In 1387 João I married **Philippa of Lancaster**, daughter of John of Gaunt, in Porto Cathedral. She brought English courtiers and customs. Their children, later called the "Ínclita Geração" (illustrious generation), included King Duarte, Prince Pedro and Prince Henry.
Using it
The alliance had rough patches, like Britain's 1890 ultimatum over African territory, which caused outrage in Portugal. But it has been invoked many times.
In 1943 neutral Portugal let the Allies use bases in the Azores, citing the old alliance; the Lajes base is still used by the US today.
A treaty signed after a medieval battle still links Lisbon and London more than 600 years later.

cards.title: The Avis dynasty
cards.text: The Avis kings launched the overseas expansion: Ceuta (1415), the Atlantic islands, the African coast and finally India. It was the start of Portugal's golden age.

deep.x: The House of Avis ruled from 1385 to 1580. With peace with Castile signed in 1411, Portugal's kings, short of land to conquer at home, looked overseas for gold, trade and crusading glory.
Why go?

Ceuta, captured in 1415, was a rich Moroccan port. It turned out to be costly to hold, but it showed what the sea could offer. Henry the Navigator then sponsored voyages down Africa's coast, and Madeira and the Azores were settled. A darker side began early: by the 1440s Portuguese ships were bringing enslaved Africans to Lagos.
The end

The dynasty ended in tragedy. King Sebastião died at Alcácer Quibir in Morocco in 1578, without an heir. His elderly great-uncle, Cardinal Henrique, reigned briefly, and in 1580 Philip II of Spain took the throne.

deep.w: Henry the Navigator ran a school of navigation at Sagres
deep.r: He rarely went to sea himself, and the "school of Sagres" is a later myth; he organised and paid for voyages

deep.x: The Avis kings turned a small kingdom into the first global sea power.

quiz.q: Which city is called "the cradle of Portugal"?
quiz.explain: Afonso Henriques' base; São Mamede was nearby.

quiz.q: Who won the Battle of Aljubarrota in 1385?
What is the Treaty of Windsor (1386)?

lessons.title: The Renaissance
lessons.summary: Rebirth of art, science and ideas.

cards.title: A rebirth
cards.text: The Renaissance ("rebirth") began in Italy in the 1300s–1400s. Scholars rediscovered Greek and Roman texts, artists studied nature and the human body, and individuals were celebrated.

deep.x: The word comes from the Italian **rinascita**, used by the painter-biographer Giorgio Vasari in 1550. "Renaissance" as the name of a whole period only caught on in the 1800s, with historians such as Jacob Burckhardt.
Why Italy?

x: Rich, independent cities competing for prestige
Roman ruins everywhere, a daily reminder of a great past
Contact with Byzantine scholars who knew Greek
Wealth from trade and banking to pay for it all

deep.x: Hunting for lost books

Scholars searched monastery libraries for forgotten Latin texts. Petrarch found letters by Cicero in Verona in 1345. In 1417 Poggio Bracciolini found Lucretius' poem On the Nature of Things, with its ancient ideas about atoms. Greek scholars, some fleeing the Ottoman advance, brought Plato and other authors little read in the West.

deep.w: The Middle Ages were dark and the Renaissance a clean break
deep.r: Medieval scholars already read Aristotle and built universities; the Renaissance grew out of them, and Petrarch's "dark ages" was partly self-promotion

deep.x: The Renaissance was Europe looking back to Greece and Rome in order to move forward.

cards.title: Florence and patrons
cards.text: Florence led the way, funded by rich families like the Medici who sponsored artists, architects and scholars. Wealth from banking and trade paid for the art.

deep.x: Florence, a city of perhaps 40,000–60,000 people after the Black Death, grew rich on wool cloth and banking. Its gold coin, the **florin**, first struck in 1252, was trusted across Europe.
The Medici

Giovanni di Bicci de' Medici founded the family bank in 1397, with branches from London to Rome; the Pope was a key client. His son Cosimo and great-grandson **Lorenzo the Magnificent** ran Florence in practice without holding a crown.
Why pay for art?

Patrons wanted to show piety, outshine rivals and, for bankers accused of usury, perhaps ease their conscience. Contracts often set exactly what was to be painted and even how much costly blue (ultramarine, made from ground lapis lazuli) to use.
Competition

Guilds commissioned work too. In 1401 the cloth merchants held a contest for new bronze doors for the Baptistery. Lorenzo Ghiberti beat Filippo Brunelleschi, and later spent 27 years on a second pair, nicknamed the "Gates of Paradise".
Brunelleschi built the cathedral dome without the usual wooden frame underneath, using a herringbone brick pattern so each ring held itself up.
In Florence, bankers' money turned rivalry into masterpieces.

cards.title: Perspective
cards.text: Artists like Brunelleschi worked out linear perspective around 1420: parallel lines meet at a vanishing point, making flat paintings look three-dimensional.

deep.x: Medieval painters often made the most important figures biggest, not the nearest ones. Around 1415–1420, **Filippo Brunelleschi** showed how to make a painting match what the eye really sees.
The experiment

He painted the Baptistery on a panel and drilled a small hole through it. Standing in the cathedral doorway, a viewer looked through the hole from the back at a mirror held in front. Lowering the mirror revealed the real building, lined up exactly with the painting.
Written down

In 1435 Leon Battista Alberti explained the method in his book On Painting, so any artist could learn it. Masaccio's Holy Trinity fresco in Florence, from about 1427, is one of the first surviving paintings to use it fully: a painted chapel seems to open into the wall.

the same person at 20 m
looks half as tall in the picture

deep.w: Nobody before 1420 painted depth
deep.r: Roman wall paintings in Pompeii show depth convincingly; what was new was an exact, geometric rule

deep.x: Perspective turned painting into a window, built with geometry.

cards.title: Leonardo da Vinci
cards.text: Painter of the Mona Lisa and The Last Supper, Leonardo (1452–1519) also filled notebooks with anatomy, flying machines, engineering and studies of water, a true "Renaissance man".

deep.x: Leonardo was born in 1452 in Vinci, near Florence, the son of a notary and a young woman not married to him. He trained in Verrocchio's workshop, then worked for the Duke of Milan, and died in 1519 at Amboise in France, as a guest of King Francis I.
Finished little, studied everything

Fewer than 20 paintings are generally accepted as his. He painted The Last Supper with an experimental mix on dry plaster instead of true fresco, so it began flaking within his lifetime. The Mona Lisa, probably Lisa Gherardini, wife of a Florentine merchant, stayed with him for years as he kept reworking it.
The notebooks
More than 7,000 pages survive. Left-handed, he wrote in mirror script, from right to left.
His anatomical drawings, based on dissecting dozens of bodies, were remarkably accurate, but stayed unpublished for centuries, so they barely influenced medicine at the time.

deep.w: Leonardo invented working helicopters and tanks
deep.r: They were sketches and ideas; most were never built and many wouldn't have worked as drawn

deep.x: The Mona Lisa became world-famous partly because it was stolen from the Louvre in 1911; it was recovered in Florence two years later.
Leonardo's genius was curiosity: he looked at everything, though he finished little.

cards.title: Michelangelo
cards.text: Michelangelo (1475–1564) sculpted David and painted the Sistine Chapel ceiling, lying on scaffolding for four years. He also designed the dome of St Peter's in Rome.

deep.x: Michelangelo Buonarroti saw himself as a sculptor first. At about 24 he carved the Pietà in St Peter's, the only work he signed. In 1501, aged 26, he began **David** from a huge block of marble other sculptors had abandoned.
The Sistine ceiling, 1508–1512

Pope Julius II pushed him into a job he didn't want. He painted in true fresco: wet plaster laid each morning, painted before it dried, so each day's patch (a giornata) had to be finished at once. The centre shows scenes from Genesis, including the Creation of Adam.
He even wrote a comic poem about the pain: neck twisted, beard pointing at the sky, paint dripping on his face.
A long life
He took over St Peter's at 71 and designed its dome, which was finished in 1590, after his death, by Giacomo della Porta. He died in 1564, aged 88, still working.
Michelangelo and Leonardo were once both asked to paint huge battle scenes in the same hall in Florence; neither finished.
Michelangelo made marble seem alive and turned a chapel ceiling into a universe.

cards.title: Humanism
cards.text: Humanists believed in studying classical texts, good writing and the potential of human beings. Erasmus of Rotterdam was its most famous northern European voice.

deep.x: The **studia humanitatis**, the "humanities", were five subjects: grammar, rhetoric, poetry, history and moral philosophy. Humanists wanted to read the classics in good original texts and write elegant Latin, and believed education made better citizens.
Reading critically

Going back to sources, **ad fontes**, could be explosive. In 1440 Lorenzo Valla showed that the "Donation of Constantine", a document used to support the Pope's claim to land, was a forgery: its Latin was centuries too late.
Erasmus

Erasmus of Rotterdam (about 1466–1536) was Europe's best-known scholar. He published a Greek New Testament in 1516 with a new Latin translation, and mocked corrupt clergy in his satire In Praise of Folly. He wanted reform, but never left the Catholic Church.
A Portuguese humanist
Damião de Góis, a diplomat and chronicler, befriended Erasmus and stayed in his house in 1534. Back in Portugal he was later tried by the Inquisition and died soon after, in unclear circumstances.

deep.w: Humanists rejected religion
deep.r: Nearly all were Christians; they wanted purer texts and better morals, including in the Church

deep.x: Humanism trusted that careful reading and good education could improve both people and society.

cards.title: Manueline style
cards.text: Portugal's own late-Gothic style, named after King Manuel I, decorates buildings with ropes, armillary spheres, sea creatures and coral, celebrating the voyages. The Jerónimos Monastery and Belém Tower are famous examples.

deep.x: Manuel I reigned from 1495 to 1521, when spices from India made Lisbon one of Europe's richest ports. The name "Manueline" was coined only in the 1800s, but the style is unmistakable: late-Gothic buildings covered in carving of the sea.

items.b: the Order that paid for voyages

deep.x: Where to see it

The Jerónimos was begun around 1501, largely funded by a tax on the spice trade, with architects Diogo de Boitaca and then João de Castilho. Vasco da Gama and Camões lie there. Both it and the Belém Tower survived the 1755 earthquake and became a UNESCO site in 1983.
Look closer

The Belém Tower (1514–1520) has a stone rhinoceros under one turret, often linked to the animal sent from India to Lisbon in 1515, famous from Albrecht Dürer's print. Tomar's chapter-house window is a riot of ropes, corks, roots and coral.
The armillary sphere from Manueline buildings is still on the Portuguese flag today.
Manueline buildings are the Age of Discovery carved in stone: Gothic bones dressed in rope and coral.

cards.title: Os Lusíadas
cards.text: Luís de Camões published Os Lusíadas in 1572, an epic poem about Vasco da Gama's voyage and Portuguese history, inspired by classical epics. Portugal's national day, 10 June, marks his death.

deep.x: Luís de Camões (about 1524–1580) lived the adventure he wrote about. He lost an eye fighting in North Africa and spent about 17 years in Asia, in Goa and probably Macau. Tradition says he swam ashore from a shipwreck in the Mekong delta holding his manuscript.
A classical epic

It opens with "As armas e os barões assinalados", echoing Virgil's Aeneid, which begins with arms and a hero. As in Homer and Virgil, the gods take sides: Venus helps the Portuguese, Bacchus works against them.
More than praise

The poem tells Portuguese history while following Gama's voyage, but it also has doubts. The Old Man of Restelo, at the departure from Belém, condemns the thirst for glory that empties the country. Camões ends by addressing young King Sebastião, urging him on to great deeds; Sebastião would die in Morocco six years later.

deep.w: 10 June is Camões's birthday
deep.r: It marks his death, on 10 June 1580; it's now the Day of Portugal, Camões and the Portuguese Communities

deep.x: Os Lusíadas turned a sea voyage into Portugal's founding epic, with a voice of doubt built in.

cards.title: Printing spreads the Renaissance
cards.text: Gutenberg's press (around 1450) let books and new ideas spread fast. Venice became a printing capital; the first book printed in Portugal appeared in 1487, in Hebrew, in Faro.

deep.x: Around 1450 in Mainz, Johannes Gutenberg combined metal letters cast in a mould, an oil-based ink and a press adapted from wine presses. His Bible of about 1455 was printed in roughly 180 copies; about 49 survive.
Venice
By 1500 Venice had more printers than any other city. Aldus Manutius printed Greek and Latin classics in small, cheap formats and introduced italic type in 1501, the ancestor of the pocket paperback.

x: About 250 European towns had presses by 1500
they printed perhaps 10–20 million copies
all in about 50 years

deep.x: In Portugal

Jewish printers led the way. In 1487 Samuel Gacon printed the Pentateuch in Hebrew in Faro. In Leiria, in 1496, Abraham d'Ortas printed the astronomical tables of **Abraham Zacuto**, which Portuguese navigators used to work out latitude at sea.
Only one copy of the Faro Pentateuch is known to survive; it is in the British Library in London.
Printing turned rare ideas into common property, and fast.

cards.title: Renaissance science
cards.text: Artists' careful observation fed into science: Vesalius' accurate anatomy (1543) and Copernicus' Sun-centred universe (1543) both appeared in the same year.

deep.x: Artists measured bodies and light; navigators measured stars and coasts. That habit of careful observation fed directly into science.
1543: two books

**Andreas Vesalius**, a 28-year-old professor at Padua, published a huge illustrated anatomy, with woodcuts probably from Titian's workshop. Doctors had followed the Roman physician Galen, who mostly dissected animals. Vesalius showed many of his errors: the human jaw is one bone, not two, for example.
Portugal's contribution

Pedro Nunes, royal cosmographer, showed that a ship on a fixed compass bearing follows a spiral line, not a great circle. He also invented the **nónio**, a scale for reading tiny fractions of a degree. Garcia de Orta's book on the medicinal plants of India was one of the first European works on tropical medicine.
Old authority, new eyes
Neither Galen nor Ptolemy was thrown out overnight. But each time careful observation contradicted the ancients, trust slowly shifted from old books to evidence.
Duarte Pacheco Pereira wrote around 1505 that experience is "the mother of things", a slogan for science before the Scientific Revolution.
When people started trusting their own eyes over ancient books, science began to change.

quiz.q: Which family famously sponsored Renaissance artists in Florence?
What is the Manueline style?
options: Portugal's ornate late-Gothic architecture with maritime motifs

quiz.q: Who wrote Os Lusíadas?

lessons.title: Reformation and Scientific Revolution
lessons.summary: New ideas about faith and nature.

cards.title: Luther's 95 theses

events.l: Church of England breaks with Rome

cards.text: In 1517, the monk Martin Luther challenged the Church's sale of indulgences (payments to reduce punishment for sins). His protest, spread by printing, split western Christianity.

deep.x: Martin Luther was an Augustinian friar and theology professor in Wittenberg, Germany. An **indulgence** was a Church document that reduced the time a soul would spend in purgatory. In 1517 the preacher Johann Tetzel was selling them nearby to help pay for rebuilding St Peter's in Rome.
What Luther argued
His 95 points, in Latin, were meant for academic debate. He said forgiveness can't be bought, that the Pope had no power over purgatory, and that salvation comes through faith in God's grace.
Printing made him

Within weeks, printers turned his theses and pamphlets into German, with woodcut cartoons for people who couldn't read well. Luther became the best-selling author of his time. At the Diet of Worms in 1521 he refused to take back his writings before Emperor Charles V and was declared an outlaw.
Hidden in a castle

His prince, Frederick the Wise, had him "kidnapped" for his own safety and hidden in Wartburg Castle. There Luther translated the New Testament into German in about 11 weeks. His Bible helped shape the modern German language.

deep.w: Luther nailed his theses to a church door with a hammer
deep.r: It may have happened, but the story first appears after his death; he certainly sent them to the archbishop on 31 October 1517

deep.x: A protest about money became a split in Christianity because printing carried it everywhere.

cards.title: Protestant and Catholic
cards.text: Protestants stressed faith and the Bible read in people's own languages; the Catholic Church responded with the Counter-Reformation, reforming itself and founding orders like the Jesuits.

deep.x: The name **Protestant** comes from a formal protest by Lutheran princes in 1529. The movement soon split into several branches.
The main differences
The Catholic response

The **Council of Trent** (1545–1563) restated Catholic doctrine, tightened discipline and ordered seminaries to train priests properly. The Church also listed forbidden books from 1559 and used grand Baroque art and music to inspire the faithful.
The Jesuits

Ignatius of Loyola, a Basque ex-soldier, founded the Society of Jesus, approved in 1540. Among its first members was the Portuguese Simão Rodrigues. King João III of Portugal was an early supporter: in 1541 Francis Xavier sailed from Lisbon to India. Jesuits ran schools and universities, including Évora's university from 1559, and sent missionaries to Brazil, Japan and China.

deep.w: The Counter-Reformation was only a reaction
deep.r: Catholic reform had started before Luther, in Spain and Italy; Trent sped it up and gave it shape

deep.x: Protestants put scripture in everyone's hands; Catholics answered by reforming, teaching and sending missions worldwide.

cards.title: Wars of religion
cards.text: Religious division fuelled wars across Europe for over a century, culminating in the devastating Thirty Years' War (1618–1648), which killed millions in central Europe.

deep.x: In the 1500s most people believed a state needed one religion to hold together. When subjects and rulers disagreed, religion mixed with politics, dynasties and money, and war followed.
France and the Netherlands

In France, Catholics and Protestant Huguenots fought eight wars. In the St Bartholomew's Day massacre of 1572, thousands of Protestants were killed. The Edict of Nantes in 1598 gave Huguenots limited tolerance. The Dutch fought Spain for 80 years, partly over religion, and won independence in 1648.
The Thirty Years' War

It began in 1618 when Protestant nobles in Prague threw two Catholic officials out of a castle window. It grew into a European war involving Sweden, France, Spain and the Habsburg emperor; Catholic France even backed Protestants to weaken the Habsburgs.
Most victims died not in battle but from hunger, plague and armies living off the land.
The peace
The Peace of Westphalia (1648) let rulers choose their state's religion and treated states as sovereign, a principle of international law still cited today.
Portugal's war to regain independence from Spain began in 1640, when Spain was stretched thin by the Thirty Years' War.
Europe learnt through a century of slaughter that faith could not be imposed by force.

cards.title: The Inquisition in Portugal

events.l: Jews ordered to convert or leave

cards.text: The Portuguese Inquisition, established in 1536, persecuted New Christians (converted Jews), suspected heretics and others. Many Jewish families fled to the Netherlands, Ottoman lands and elsewhere. It was abolished in 1821.

deep.x: In 1496–97 King Manuel I ordered Portugal's Jews to leave, then forced most of them to be baptised so they would stay. They became **New Christians**. Many were suspected of secretly practising Judaism, and in 1506 a mob in Lisbon killed perhaps 2,000 or more of them.
How it worked

King João III asked the Pope for an Inquisition, granted in 1536. Tribunals sat in Lisbon, Évora, Coimbra and, from 1560, Goa. Accusations were often anonymous; torture was used; property was confiscated. Sentences were read at public ceremonies called **autos-da-fé**.
The diaspora
Many New Christian families fled, taking skills and trade networks with them.
The philosopher Spinoza was born in Amsterdam in 1632 to a Portuguese-Jewish family. Jesuit Father António Vieira, who criticised the Inquisition, was himself tried by it in the 1660s.
In Belmonte, in Beira Interior, a community kept Jewish practices in secret for more than 400 years, until it was revealed in the 20th century.
Portugal's Inquisition drove out many of its most enterprising families, and other countries gained what Portugal lost.

cards.title: Copernicus
cards.text: In 1543 Copernicus argued that Earth and the planets orbit the Sun, not the other way round. It was a radical idea that took over a century to be widely accepted.

deep.x: Nicolaus Copernicus (1473–1543) was a Polish churchman, doctor and astronomer. The Greek Aristarchus had suggested a Sun-centred system around 250 BCE, but **Ptolemy**'s Earth-centred model ruled for about 1,400 years.
Why it was attractive

Planets like Mars sometimes seem to move backwards across the sky for a few weeks. Ptolemy explained this with small circles on circles. Copernicus showed it happens naturally when the faster Earth overtakes Mars. His model also put the planets in a clear order with sizes of orbits that could be calculated.
Why people hesitated

x: His orbits were still perfect circles, so he still needed epicycles and was no more accurate than Ptolemy
If Earth moved, the stars should shift slightly through the year; nobody could see that until 1838
It clashed with everyday experience and with some Bible passages
Earth's orbit is about 940 million km
÷ 365 days × 24 h
≈ 107,000 km/h, or about 30 km/s

deep.w: The Church banned Copernicus at once
deep.r: His book circulated freely for 73 years; it was put on the list of forbidden books only in 1616, "until corrected"

deep.x: Copernicus moved Earth from the centre, but it took others to prove he was right.

cards.title: Galileo's trial
cards.text: Galileo's telescope observations supported Copernicus. In 1633 the Roman Inquisition forced him to recant and kept him under house arrest. The Church formally acknowledged its error in 1992.

deep.x: In 1609 Galileo Galilei, a professor at Padua, heard of a Dutch spyglass and built his own, eventually magnifying about 20–30 times. Pointing it at the sky, he saw things no one had seen.
Why Venus mattered
In Ptolemy's model Venus could never appear full. Galileo saw it go through all its phases, like the Moon. That fitted Venus orbiting the Sun.
The trial

In 1616 the Church warned Galileo not to hold or defend Copernicus' view. In 1632 he published a Dialogue in which the Earth-centred view was voiced by a character named Simplicio, which Pope Urban VIII, once his friend, took as mockery.

Aged 69, under threat of torture, he formally renounced the idea on 22 June 1633. He spent his last years under house arrest near Florence, where he wrote his great book on motion, smuggled out and printed in the Netherlands in 1638.

deep.w: Galileo muttered "And yet it moves" as he left the court
deep.r: The line first appears more than a century later and is almost certainly invented

deep.x: Galileo's trial became a symbol of authority clashing with evidence, though the evidence won in the end.

cards.title: The scientific method
cards.text: Thinkers like Francis Bacon and Descartes argued for learning through observation, experiment and reason rather than authority alone. This became the scientific method.

deep.x: For centuries, learning meant mastering authorities: Aristotle on nature, Galen on medicine. In the 1600s thinkers asked a sharper question: how do we actually know?
Bacon

The English lawyer Francis Bacon, in his Novum Organum (1620), urged people to gather facts systematically and test them with experiments. He warned of "idols", the habits that distort our thinking, such as seeing what we expect to see.
Descartes
The French philosopher René Descartes, in his Discourse on the Method (1637), began by doubting everything he could, and rebuilt knowledge step by step on clear reasoning and mathematics.
Putting it together
Modern science combines both: experiments to check ideas against nature, and maths to make precise predictions.

x: A good theory makes predictions that could turn out wrong
Results must be repeatable by others
Measurement beats opinion, even an expert's

deep.x: Bacon is said to have died in 1626 after catching a chill while stuffing a chicken with snow to see if cold preserved meat; the story may be embroidered.
Science became a method, not a set of books: test ideas against nature and let the results decide.

cards.title: Newton's synthesis
cards.text: Newton's Principia (1687) used a few laws to explain both falling objects and planetary orbits. It showed the universe follows mathematical rules, a turning point for science.

deep.x: Isaac Newton's **Philosophiae Naturalis Principia Mathematica** ("Mathematical Principles of Natural Philosophy") appeared in Latin in 1687. Edmond Halley, of comet fame, urged him to write it and paid for its printing.

items.b: no force, no change of motion
every push has a push back

deep.x: The big idea

The same force that pulls an apple down keeps the Moon in orbit. Gravity weakens with the square of distance, and with that one rule Newton explained Kepler's elliptical orbits, the tides and the paths of comets.

x: The Moon is about 60 Earth radii away
gravity there is 60 × 60 = 3,600 times weaker
9.8 ÷ 3,600 ≈ 0.0027 m/s², matching the Moon's orbit

deep.x: Afterwards

Using Newton's methods, Halley predicted that a comet would return in 1758. It did, after his death, and now bears his name. Newton also invented calculus, at about the same time as the German Leibniz, which led to a bitter fight over who came first.

deep.w: Einstein proved Newton wrong
deep.r: Einstein refined Newton for extreme speeds and gravity; Newton's laws still guide spacecraft

deep.x: Newton showed that the heavens and the Earth follow the same few mathematical rules.

cards.title: Scientific societies
cards.text: Groups like the Royal Society in London (1660) and the French Academy of Sciences (1666) met to share experiments and published journals, the start of modern peer-reviewed science.

deep.x: Before journals, scientists shared work by private letters, slowly and unevenly. Societies made it public and regular.
The Royal Society

Founded in London in 1660, with a royal charter from 1662, its motto is **Nullius in verba**, "take nobody's word for it". Members watched experiments performed in front of them, often by its curator, Robert Hooke. Newton was its president from 1703 until his death.
Different models
Journals

Philosophical Transactions, first published in 1665, is the world's oldest scientific journal still running. Publishing gave a clear date to discoveries, so priority could be settled and results checked by others.

deep.w: Peer review began in 1665
deep.r: Journals then had editors; systematic review by outside experts became standard only in the 20th century

deep.x: Portugal's Academy of Sciences of Lisbon was founded in 1779, and it still meets today.
Science became a shared, public conversation, where claims had to survive other people's checks.

cards.title: Instruments
cards.text: Telescopes, microscopes, thermometers, barometers and pendulum clocks let scientists measure what they couldn't see before.

deep.x: Instruments did two things: they extended the senses, and they turned qualities into numbers. "Warm" became 25 °C; "heavy air" became a height of mercury.
Seeing the small

Robert Hooke's Micrographia (1665) showed a flea in huge detail and used the word "cell" for the tiny boxes he saw in cork. The Dutch draper Antonie van Leeuwenhoek, with tiny single lenses, saw bacteria in 1676.
Measuring air

Evangelista Torricelli filled a glass tube with mercury and turned it upside down in a dish: the column fell to about 76 cm. The weight of the air held the rest up. In 1648 Pascal's brother-in-law carried one up a mountain and the column was lower at the top.

x: Mercury is 13.6 times denser than water
a water barometer would need a tube about 10.3 m tall

deep.x: Keeping time
Pedro Nunes' nónio (1542), a scale for reading fractions of a degree, is an ancestor of the vernier on today's callipers; in Portuguese it is still called a nónio.
New instruments turned guesses into measurements, and measurement became the language of science.

quiz.q: What did Luther protest against in 1517?
Copernicus proposed that…
What does the scientific method rely on?

lessons.title: The 1755 earthquake and the Enlightenment
lessons.summary: Lisbon destroyed, rebuilt and rethought.

cards.title: 1 November 1755
cards.text: On All Saints' Day morning, a huge earthquake struck off Portugal's coast. Churches were full and candles lit. Within minutes much of Lisbon collapsed.

deep.x: The first shock hit at about 9:40 in the morning. Lisbon was one of Europe's richest ports, with perhaps 200,000 people, and on a holy day most of them were at Mass. Stone churches packed with worshippers were among the deadliest places to be.
Minutes of chaos

Witnesses described three separate shocks lasting in total somewhere between about three and six minutes. Cracks several metres wide opened in the city centre. Roofs and vaults fell on the congregations, and narrow medieval streets filled with rubble, trapping people who ran outside.

x: Many fled to the open riverside at Terreiro do Paço, the palace square
The royal family survived because they were away at Belém, then outside the city
King José I was so shaken that he reportedly refused to live under stone roofs again, and the court lived in tents and wooden buildings for years

deep.x: What was lost

The Ribeira Palace on the river collapsed with its royal library of tens of thousands of books, archives of the voyages of discovery and paintings by masters such as Titian and Rubens. A grand new opera house, opened only months before, was destroyed. The ruined Carmo Convent, still roofless above the Baixa, is the best place to picture the day.
The earthquake struck at the worst possible moment: a holy day, a full city and burning candles in every church.
The shaking was felt as far away as southern France and North Africa, and some lakes in Scandinavia were reported to slosh oddly that morning.

cards.title: Earthquake, tsunami, fire
cards.text: The earthquake, estimated at magnitude 8.5–9, was followed by a tsunami up to several metres high and by fires that burned for days. Estimates of deaths in Lisbon range from about 30,000 to 50,000 or more.

deep.x: Lisbon suffered three disasters in a row, each making the next worse. The epicentre lay in the Atlantic, probably a couple of hundred kilometres south-west of Cape St Vincent, where the African and Eurasian plates meet. Its exact location is still debated.
The wave

Around 40 minutes after the shaking, survivors who had gathered on the riverbank saw the Tagus draw back, exposing the riverbed and old wrecks. Then the sea rushed in. In Lisbon the waves reached about 5–6 metres; in parts of the Algarve, such as Lagos, they may have been higher still. The tsunami also hit Cádiz and Morocco and was recorded across the Atlantic in the Caribbean.
The fire

Overturned candles, kitchen hearths and looters started fires that merged into a firestorm. It burned for about five or six days and destroyed much of what the shaking had left standing, including warehouses full of goods from Brazil and Asia.

x: Estimates of the dead in Lisbon range from about 30,000 to 50,000 or more
Thousands more died in the Algarve, Spain and Morocco
Records were themselves destroyed, which is why figures remain uncertain

deep.x: Most victims died not in one event but in a chain: falling stone, then water, then fire.

deep.w: Most people died in the tsunami
deep.r: The collapse of buildings and the fires probably killed more people than the wave in Lisbon itself

cards.title: The Marquis of Pombal
cards.text: Sebastião José de Carvalho e Melo, later Marquis of Pombal, led the response: "bury the dead and feed the living". He organised relief, controlled prices and planned the rebuilding.

deep.x: Sebastião José de Carvalho e Melo (1699–1782) was a former diplomat in London and Vienna who had become one of King José I's ministers in 1750. While others saw divine punishment, he treated the disaster as a practical problem. The famous phrase "bury the dead and feed the living" is attributed to him, though some historians credit it to another nobleman.
The emergency plan

items.b: sunk at sea to stop disease
price caps, tax waived on grain
no new building till a plan

deep.x: Within days, troops ringed the city to stop people leaving and to catch looters. Food was brought in by sea, and its prices were fixed. Building was frozen until engineers could prepare a new plan, so that landowners could not simply rebuild the old maze.
Power and its price

The crisis made Carvalho e Melo the most powerful man in Portugal for 22 years. He became Count of Oeiras in 1759 and Marquis of Pombal only in 1769, so the name we use came much later. He ruled with a hard hand: after an attempt on the king's life in 1758, members of the noble Távora family were executed publicly in Belém in 1759.
When José I died in 1777, Queen Maria I dismissed him. Hundreds of political prisoners were released, and he was exiled to his estate at Pombal.
Pombal was both a brilliant crisis manager and a ruthless autocrat, and Portugal remembers him as both.

cards.title: The new Baixa
cards.text: The Baixa was rebuilt on a grid of wide straight streets with uniform buildings, using standardised parts and the earthquake-resistant gaiola pombalina.

deep.x: The flattened lower town between Rossio and the river was not patched up but redesigned. The chief engineer, Manuel da Maia, then in his late seventies, drew up several options, from rebuilding as before to moving the capital. The chosen plan, drawn by Eugénio dos Santos and Carlos Mardel, wiped the slate clean.
The gaiola pombalina

Inside the stone walls of each building stands a wooden "cage": a three-dimensional frame of posts and beams braced with diagonal crosses. Masonry holds it in place, but in an earthquake the timber flexes and keeps the building together instead of letting walls burst outwards. According to tradition, a model was tested by soldiers marching around it to imitate shaking.
An early prefab city

Windows, doors, iron railings and tiles came in a few standard sizes, made off-site and assembled quickly. Streets were named after trades: Rua do Ouro for goldsmiths, Rua da Prata for silversmiths, Rua dos Fanqueiros for cloth sellers. The palace square became Praça do Comércio, the "square of commerce", a sign that trade, not the court, would own the riverfront.
The Baixa was one of the first city centres planned to resist earthquakes, built from standard parts on a rational grid.
The buildings stand on thousands of pine stakes driven into waterlogged ground. As long as they stay wet they barely rot, which is why lowering the water table is a real concern.

cards.title: The birth of seismology
cards.text: Pombal sent a questionnaire to every parish: when did it start, how long did it last, what damage occurred? It was one of the first systematic scientific studies of an earthquake.

deep.x: Before 1755, earthquakes were mostly explained as acts of God or by vague ideas about underground winds. Pombal's government did something new: it asked the same set of questions everywhere and collected the answers. That is the basic method of modern science.
The questionnaire
Through the Church, every parish priest in the country received a list of questions. They included:

items: Where did it seem to come from?
Did the sea or wells change?

deep.x: Many of the answers survive in the national archive, the Torre do Tombo, in a collection known as the parish memories of 1758. Modern seismologists have used them to map how strongly each place shook, and from that to estimate the epicentre and size.

x: Collect reports of damage per parish
Draw lines of equal intensity on a map
Strongest shaking points towards the source offshore

deep.x: From stories to science

x: In 1756 the young Immanuel Kant wrote three essays seeking natural causes for the quake
In 1760 the English geologist John Michell argued earthquakes were waves travelling through the ground, partly using Lisbon data
Seismometers came only in the 19th century, but the idea of systematic observation started here

deep.x: By asking every parish the same questions, Portugal turned a catastrophe into data.

deep.w: The 1755 magnitude was measured at the time
deep.r: Magnitude scales date from the 1930s; the 8.5–9 figure is a modern estimate from historical reports

cards.title: Shaking European thought
cards.text: The disaster shocked Europe's thinkers. Voltaire questioned why a good God would allow it, in his "Poem on the Lisbon Disaster" and in Candide. Rousseau answered that city crowding made it worse.

deep.x: Before 1755, a popular philosophy called optimism, linked to Leibniz and the poet Alexander Pope, held that we live in the best of all possible worlds and that every evil serves a larger good. Lisbon made that idea very hard to defend. Why would a good God destroy a pious city, on a holy day, while worshippers prayed?
Voltaire against optimism

In his "Poem on the Lisbon Disaster" Voltaire asked whether Lisbon really had more vices than London or Paris, which still stood. In Candide (1759) he satirised optimism: his naïve heroes arrive in Lisbon during the earthquake, then watch the Inquisition burn people to prevent further quakes, while their tutor Pangloss insists all is for the best.
Rousseau's reply

Rousseau wrote to Voltaire that nature had not built 20,000 houses of six or seven storeys in one place. If people had lived more spread out, and had not stayed behind to save their belongings, far fewer would have died. It is an early argument that "natural" disasters are partly made by human choices.

The Jesuit preacher Gabriel Malagrida insisted the quake was divine punishment and blamed sinners. Pombal, who favoured practical measures, saw this as a threat; Malagrida was later burned by the Inquisition in 1761.
Lisbon 1755 pushed European thinkers from asking why God allows disasters to asking how humans can reduce them.

cards.title: The Enlightenment
cards.text: The 18th-century Enlightenment championed reason, science, religious tolerance and individual rights. Thinkers like Locke, Montesquieu, Voltaire and Kant inspired revolutions.

deep.x: The Enlightenment was a movement of ideas across 18th-century Europe and its colonies. Its core belief was that human reason, not tradition or religious authority alone, should guide how we understand nature and organise society. Kant summed it up in 1784 with the motto "dare to know".
Big ideas

x: Government gets its legitimacy from the people, not from God
Power should be split between those who make, apply and judge laws
Torture and cruel punishments are irrational (Beccaria, 1764)
Free trade and markets can create wealth (Adam Smith, 1776)

deep.x: These ideas spread through books, newspapers, scientific academies, salons and coffee houses, where people of different ranks could debate.
Portugal's version

Portuguese reformers, often called "estrangeirados" because they had lived abroad, brought these ideas home. Luís António Verney's book on "the true method of studying" (1746) attacked old-fashioned teaching. Pombal, like Frederick the Great of Prussia or Catherine the Great of Russia, was an **enlightened despot**: he used reason to modernise, but kept absolute power.
The Enlightenment taught that the world can be understood and society can be improved by reason, an idea behind modern science and democracy.

deep.w: Enlightenment thinkers all wanted democracy
deep.r: Many, like Voltaire, preferred a wise king to rule by the people

cards.title: Pombal's reforms
cards.text: Pombal modernised education and trade, expelled the Jesuits (1759), created the Douro wine demarcation (1756), one of the world's first, and reduced discrimination against New Christians.

deep.x: Pombal wanted a stronger, richer state that depended less on Britain and on the nobility and the Church. His reforms touched trade, schools, religion and law, and many still shape Portugal today.
Port wine and the Douro

British merchants dominated the port trade, and quality was falling as cheap wine was mixed in. In 1756 Pombal created a royal company to control production and marked the boundaries of the Douro vineyards with granite posts, many still standing. It is one of the world's oldest regulated wine regions, alongside earlier efforts in Tokaj and Chianti.
Church and education

The Jesuits ran most schools and had great influence at court. Pombal accused them of plotting and expelled them from Portugal and the empire in 1759, before France and Spain did the same. The state then had to build its own school system. The University of Coimbra was reformed in 1772, gaining mathematics and natural science faculties, a botanical garden, an observatory and laboratories.
Society

New Christians, descendants of Jews forced to convert in 1497, had faced discrimination for centuries; in 1773 the legal distinction was abolished. In 1761 Pombal banned bringing enslaved people into mainland Portugal, though slavery continued in Brazil and Africa.
Pombal modernised Portugal from the top down, with reforms that were bold, lasting and imposed without consent.
The granite boundary markers of 1758–61 are known as "marcos pombalinos", and over a hundred survive in the Douro vineyards.

cards.title: The Encyclopédie
cards.text: Diderot and d'Alembert's Encyclopédie (1751–1772) gathered knowledge on everything from trades to philosophy, spreading Enlightenment ideas across Europe.
